notes.observation: Immediately after the repeated heading, both the pinned chapter extraction and retained page-37 text witness begin only with '-ம் ஆண்டு,'; the year numerals are absent from the digital text. Independent biographical sources place this exact Tiruvarur High School admission episode in 1936, consistent with Kalaignar being twelve years old as the passage states.
notes.translation_action: T1 reconstructs the opening explicitly as 'In 1936' and keeps this intervention documented. The translation does not present the digital source as though it contained the numerals, and the read-only source remains unchanged.

notes.observation: The digital source/page witness gives the headmaster's name as 'கர்ஸ்தூரி ஐயங்கார்'. Independent biographical references to the same admission episode give Kasthuri/Kasturi Iyengar.
notes.translation_action: T1 uses the externally corroborated personal-name form 'Kasthuri Iyengar' in English while preserving this note about the digital-source spelling. This is a name-normalisation decision, not a source correction.

notes.observation: Headmaster Iyengar asks 'என்ன வேணும் நோக்கு?'. As established independently in v1-ch03 for Postmaster Iyer, dated Brahmin-Tamil 'நோக்கு' functions as 'உனக்கு' ('for/to you'), not the ordinary verb 'look'.
notes.translation_action: T1 translates by function ('What do you want?') without inventing an English caste or regional accent.

notes.observation: The school scene includes colonial-period terms 'பங்கா' and 'பியூன்': a punkah being pulled at the doorway and the peon who tries to stop the boy.
notes.translation_action: T1 retains 'punkah' and 'peon' to preserve the period scene rather than replacing them with generic modern equivalents.

notes.observation: Kalaignar narrates the admission episode in third-person dramatic present: a twelve-year-old boy bursts into the headmaster's room, argues for admission, threatens to jump into Kamalalayam, wins a place, celebrates with his father, and only afterward asks the reader who the boy was before revealing 'நானே தான்!'
notes.translation_action: T1 preserves the third-person dramatic present, dialogue, suspense, reader-address and delayed self-reveal; it does not reveal 'I' early.

notes.observation: On page 37, after the headmaster says 'அதற்கு நான் என்ன செய்வது தம்பி?', the boy's next plea begins 'உயர் நிலைப்பள்ளியில் சேராமல் ஊருக்குத் திரும்பினால்...' but the opening quotation mark is missing while a closing quotation mark remains.
notes.translation_action: T1 treats the passage as the boy's continuing direct speech and restores quotation structure in English.

notes.observation: Page 38 reads 'வழுக்கி விழுத்து' in the description of people slipping on the moss-covered tank steps. Context requires the ordinary falling sense represented by 'விழுந்து'.
notes.translation_action: T1 translates the secure contextual action ('slipped ... fallen in') while retaining this note; the Tamil source is not altered.

notes.observation: Page 38 reads 'ஐந்தாம் வகுப்பில் முதன்மையான மார்க்குகள் பெற்று அந்த ஆண்டு. அந்தப் பையன் வெற்றி பெற்றான்.' The full stop interrupts a syntactically continuous statement about the boy passing that year with leading/top marks.
notes.translation_action: T1 reconstructs the continuous sentence in English; T3 uses idiomatic 'top marks'.

notes.observation: Page 38 contains 'அந்தக் சுட்சியின் கொள்கைகளை வெளியிடவும், பரப்பவும்' immediately after the formation of the political party. The contextual referent is unequivocally the party and its policies; 'சுட்சி' is anomalous in this digital witness.
notes.translation_action: T1 translates the contextually secure sense 'the policies of that party' and retains the source form in this note.

notes.observation: Page 39 gives 'சட்டசயைத் தலைவராக' in the office held by Sir P. Rajagopalachariar. The surrounding political-administrative sentence clearly requires the legislative-body sense 'சட்டசபைத்'.
notes.translation_action: T2 normalises the English institutional title to 'President of the Legislative Council' because the 1920s Madras Presidency institution was the Legislative Council; the source wording remains documented.

notes.observation: Page 41 says that after Nair, Thiagarayar and the Raja of Panagal died in succession, 'நீதிக்கட்சி கலகலத்து நின்றது'. Lexical evidence for 'கலகல' includes becoming shaky or losing strength, so the wording need not be treated as corrupt merely because its more familiar modern sense relates to liveliness/noise.
notes.translation_action: T3 preserves the political weakening and physical image as 'the Justice Party stood shaken', replacing only the stiff T1/T2 syntax 'was left standing shaken'.

notes.observation: The source gives the Tamil name 'தென்னிந்திய நல உரிமைச் சங்கம்'. Independent historical and educational sources identify its historically attested English proper name as 'South Indian Liberal Federation (SILF)', popularly known as the Justice Party after its English daily Justice.
notes.translation_action: T2 uses 'South Indian Liberal Federation' in English. This is a proper-name normalisation for scholarly reader accuracy, not a correction of Kalaignar's historical account.

notes.observation: The chapter uses historically loaded movement vocabulary including 'திராவிடப் பெருங்குடி மக்கள்', 'ஜஸ்டிஸ் கட்சி' / 'நீதிக் கட்சி', 'தாழ்த்தப்பட்ட மக்கள்', 'சுயாட்சி', 'சுயமரியாதை இயக்கம்', 'பகுத்தறிவு', and the relation between Periyar, Anna and the Justice Party.
notes.translation_action: T2 freezes context-sensitive working forms: 'great Dravidian community', 'Justice Party', 'depressed communities/people', 'self-government' or 'Swaraj Party' as context requires, 'Self-Respect Movement', and 'rationalism'.

notes.observation: The source uses 'முதல் மந்திரி', 'மந்திரி சபை', and 'சட்டசபைத் தலைவர்' for 1920s Madras Presidency institutions, and calls Edwin Montagu 'இந்தியா மந்திரி' in the 1917 passage.
notes.translation_action: T2 retains the period office title 'First Minister', uses 'ministry' for 'மந்திரி சபை', and renders 'சட்டசபைத் தலைவர்' as 'President of the Legislative Council'. T3 renders Montagu's office by its attested official English title 'Secretary of State for India' rather than the unnatural literal 'India Minister'. These are institutional normalisations, not historical fact-corrections.

notes.observation: The T1/T2 Home Rule comparison contained the added phrase 'in their view', but the Tamil directly asserts that the Justice Party statement revealed the true condition of Dravidian society. T1/T2 also used English 'schemes' for neutral Tamil 'திட்டங்கள்'.
notes.translation_action: T3 removes the unsupported hedge and uses neutral 'plans', restoring Kalaignar's direct political assertion without strengthening it beyond the source.

notes.observation: The chapter title and the Panagal Raja passage use 'அரிச்சுவடி'—the alphabet/primer—as a metaphor for Kalaignar's first political education.
notes.translation_action: T1/T2/T3 retain 'primer' as the governing metaphor in the title and body.

notes.translation_action: The T1/T2/T3 translation and the dedicated thought-structure audit preserve the autobiographical-to-political expansion and keep the history anchored to the schoolbook that became Kalaignar's political primer.

external_contextual_evidence.finding: Independent biographical sources place Kalaignar's move/admission to Tiruvarur High School in 1936 at age twelve; this supports reconstruction of the missing numerals before '-ம் ஆண்டு'.
Independent accounts of the same episode identify the headmaster as Kasthuri/Kasturi Iyengar, supporting English name normalisation while the digital source form remains documented.

Historical and Tamil Nadu educational sources identify the organisation's English proper name as South Indian Liberal Federation (SILF), popularly known as the Justice Party after the English daily Justice.

Historical references for the 1920s Madras Presidency support 'First Minister' and the Legislative Council presidential office; contemporary UK parliamentary records identify Edwin Montagu's 1917 office as Secretary of State for India.
Lexical evidence includes 'become shaky / lose strength', fitting the Justice Party context.
